lesson.title: One Shared Pair: The Simplest Covalent Bond
lesson.summary: A single bond is a covalent bond formed by one shared pair of electrons between two atoms, the most common and the longest and weakest type of bond that can form between any two given atoms.
lesson.body:
Among the tools a Lewis structure has for connecting atoms, the single bond is the simplest: one pair of electrons, two electrons total, shared between two atoms and counted toward both atoms' octets at once. In a Lewis structure, a single bond is drawn either as two dots between the atoms' symbols or, more commonly in a condensed structural formula, as a single line connecting them, which is why the shorthand H-H or Cl-Cl is understood to represent a fully drawn-out shared electron pair without needing to draw the dots explicitly.

The simplest possible example is H2, hydrogen gas. Each hydrogen atom brings one valence electron, for a total of two, and both electrons are shared equally between the two nuclei as a single bonding pair. This single shared pair gives each hydrogen atom two electrons in its vicinity, satisfying the duet rule that governs hydrogen instead of the octet rule that governs larger atoms. Chlorine gas, Cl2, works the same way at a bigger scale: each chlorine atom contributes one unpaired valence electron to a shared bonding pair, while the remaining six valence electrons on each atom stay behind as three lone pairs, giving each chlorine a full octet, three lone pairs plus one bonding pair.

Methane, CH4, shows a central atom forming several single bonds at once. Carbon contributes four valence electrons and each of the four hydrogen atoms contributes one, for a total of eight electrons distributed into four separate C-H single bonds. Carbon ends up with four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, a full octet, eight electrons total, and each hydrogen ends up with one bonding pair, a full duet. No lone pairs are needed anywhere in this structure because the electron count divides up perfectly among the four single bonds.

Single bonds are the longest and weakest bonds that can form between any two particular atoms, a fact that becomes important once double and triple bonds enter the picture. A typical carbon-carbon single bond has a bond length of about 154 picometers and a bond energy of about 347 kilojoules per mole, meaning that much energy must be supplied to break one mole of those bonds apart. Because a single bond involves only one shared pair pulling the two nuclei together, the electrostatic attraction holding the bond together is weaker, and the equilibrium distance between the two nuclei is correspondingly longer, than what happens when a second shared pair is added between the same two atoms.

Single bonds are also the default starting point in the Lewis structure procedure covered earlier: every skeleton begins with single bonds connecting each pair of bonded atoms, and only gets upgraded to double or triple bonds afterward, and only when a single bonding pair alone leaves the central atom short of a full octet. Recognizing when that upgrade is necessary, and what a double bond actually looks like once it forms, is the subject of the next section.
